duree.q: How long have you been together?

engagement.q: Are you married or in a civil partnership?

enfants.q: Do you have children together (or a baby on the way)?

enfantsAvant.q: Does either of you have children from a previous relationship?

proprio.q: Do you own your home together?

quotidien.intro: Chores, tidiness, the rhythm of the week. It's usually the small things that cause the big arguments, so we start here.

rapport.fort: Day to day, you work the same way. That's rarer than people think, and it saves you a lot of small frictions.
rapport.moyen: Daily life goes fairly well, with a few different habits. Nothing serious, but these are exactly the things that get a little more annoying every week if nobody talks about them.
rapport.faible: You don't have the same idea of life at home. It's very common, and it gets much better with a few simple rules you set together, instead of settling each disagreement when it annoys you.

quo1.q: At home, who does most of the housework (cleaning, laundry, shopping, cooking)?
quo1.pourquoi: In almost every couple, each person sees what they do more clearly than what the other does. That's not a problem in itself. It becomes one when one of you feels they're carrying the house alone.
parler: If we listed everything that got done this week, who would have done what?
Which chore do you hate the most, and which one don't you mind?
quo1.eviter: Keeping score ("I did three loads of laundry"): you end up negotiating instead of organising.

quo1b.q: If you moved in together tomorrow, who do you think would do most of the housework?
quo1b.pourquoi: Before moving in, each person often has a pretty clear idea of what the other will do, without ever having talked about it. It's one of the first sources of tension once you share a roof.
parler: How was it split at your parents' place? Would you want the same, or the opposite?
What do you like doing around a home, and what do you really not want to do?
quo1b.eviter: Assuming it'll sort itself out: it rarely does, and almost never fifty-fifty.

quo2.q: Who keeps track of everything that needs doing (appointments, bills, presents, what's missing in the fridge)?
quo2.pourquoi: Doing a task and remembering it needs doing are two different things. The person who keeps track of everything often feels alone, even when the other one is happy to help as soon as they're asked.
parler: What's on your mind for the house right now that I might not see?
Is there one area I could take over completely, from start to finish?
quo2.eviter: Saying "you just have to ask me": having to ask is exactly what weighs on people.

quo2b.q: Who organises most of your time together (outings, weekends, bookings)?
quo2b.pourquoi: When you don't live together, every moment you share has to be planned. If it's always the same person doing it, they end up wondering if the other cares as much.
parler: Do you like organising, or do you do it because otherwise nobody would?
Next time we go out, who plans it, and what do we do?
quo2b.eviter: Turning it into a proof of love ("if you cared, you'd plan something"): some people just don't like planning.

quo3.q: When it comes to tidiness at home, for you...
o: A bit of mess doesn't bother me
quo3.pourquoi: The mess is almost never the real issue. For one person it's extra stress, for the other it's a home that's lived in. Without a shared rule, the one who can't stand the mess ends up tidying everything, and resenting the other.
parler: Which part of the home would you like to see tidy all the time?
What do I leave lying around that annoys you, that you've never mentioned?
quo3.eviter: Tidying the other's things with a sigh: the message gets through, but badly.

quo4.q: On weeknights, you like to go to bed...
quo4.pourquoi: A couple who don't go to bed at the same time often lose, without noticing, the moments when they talk and touch. It's fine if you know it and keep a few evenings together.
parler: Which nights of the week could we go to bed at the same time?
What do you like doing in the evening when I'm already asleep?
quo4.eviter: Criticising the other's rhythm: a night owl doesn't become an early bird to please you.

quo5.q: An ideal weekend is one that's...
o: With one or two things planned
quo5.pourquoi: The weekend is often your only real free time together. If one of you wants to fill it and the other wants to empty it, you each spend your Saturdays frustrating the other without meaning to.
parler: What does your perfect Sunday look like, from waking up to going to bed?
One weekend your way, the next one mine: how would that sound?
quo5.eviter: Announcing the plan on Friday night without asking: for the one who wanted to rest, it's already ruined.

quo6.q: Having people over (friends, family, dinners, drinks), you like it...
quo6.pourquoi: For one person, a full house is what life's about. For the other, home is the only place to breathe. And hosting takes work, which doesn't always fall on the person who invited.
parler: Ideally, how many times a month would you like us to have people over?
When we host, who does what, and are you OK with that?
quo6.eviter: Inviting people without telling the other "because it's just friends".

quo7.pourquoi: A pet means ten to fifteen years of life together, holidays planned differently, a budget and sometimes an allergy. A firm "no" on one side and a dream of a dog on the other can't be solved with a compromise.
parler: If we got a pet, which one would it be, and who'd look after it day to day?
What makes you want a pet, or what puts you off?
quo7.eviter: Adopting one and presenting the other with a done deal: the pet becomes the symbol of the argument for years.

quo7b.q: Your pet, at home, is allowed...
quo7b.pourquoi: The dog on the sofa or the cat in the bed is a detail for one person and a real annoyance for the other. And it's the kind of detail that comes back every evening.
parler: Is there a room you'd rather it stayed out of?
Who looks after it most at the moment, and are you OK with that?
quo7b.eviter: Changing the rules from one day to the next: the pet stops understanding, and so does your partner.

quo8.q: Meals, you like to have them...
quo8.pourquoi: A meal is often the only moment in the day when you're face to face. For some people it's sacred, for others it's just eating, and both ideas usually come from the family you grew up in.
parler: At your parents' place, what were meals like?
Which meal of the week could we keep just for us?
quo8.eviter: Getting into the habit of eating in front of your own screens without deciding it together.

temps.titre: Time together and time for yourself
temps.intro: How much time together, how much time apart, and what you do with it.

rapport.fort: You have the same idea of the balance between time together and time for yourself. Hold on to it: it's the first thing life eats into.
rapport.moyen: You mostly agree about time together, with a few different wishes. One or two rituals you set together are often enough to sort it out.
rapport.faible: One of you probably needs more time together, or more space, than the other. It's often felt as a lack of love when it's simply a different need.

tps1.q: Time just for the two of you (no kids, no friends, no screens), you'd like...
tps1.pourquoi: Time together is the first thing to disappear when life fills up: work, kids, friends. When one of you misses it and the other doesn't, the first one feels like they come after everything else.
parler: When was the last time we had a proper evening just for us?
What could we take out of our week to keep a moment for ourselves?
tps1.eviter: Asking for it as a reproach ("we never do anything anymore"): the other gets defensive instead of wanting to.

tps2.q: Time just for yourself, alone, you need it...
o: Very often, it's vital for me
tps2.pourquoi: Needing time alone doesn't mean loving less. But someone who never needs it can take it as rejection, and someone who needs it feels suffocated without it.
parler: When you need some quiet time, how can I tell without you having to justify it?
What does your ideal time to yourself look like?
tps2.eviter: Taking the other's need for solitude as a criticism of you.

tps3.q: Phones at the table and in bed, for you, are...
tps3.court: Phones at the table and in bed
tps3.pourquoi: Phones have become one of the most common complaints in couples, especially in the evening. It's not the object that's the problem, it's the feeling of coming second to it.
parler: At what time of day does my phone bother you most?
Shall we try one simple rule for a week, like no phones in bed?
tps3.eviter: Lecturing the other with your own phone in your hand.

o: Mostly shared, with some of our own
Mostly our own, with a few shared
tps4.pourquoi: Sharing hobbies brings you closer, keeping your own lets you stay yourself. It gets tricky when one of you experiences the other's hobbies as an absence.
parler: Is there an activity you'd like me to try?
What could we start together that neither of us has ever done?
tps4.eviter: Tagging along to the other's hobby while dragging your feet: better to leave them their moment.

tps5.q: Going out (restaurant, drinks, concert, party), you feel like it...
tps5.pourquoi: A homebody couple and a couple who go out are just as happy. It's when one wants to go out and the other wants to stay in that each ends up going out alone, or staying in frustrated.
parler: Is there an outing you dream of doing with me that we've never done?
When I say no to going out, how does that feel for you?
tps5.eviter: Saying yes reluctantly and sulking all evening.

tps6.q: A good holiday, for you, is mostly about...
tps6.pourquoi: Holidays are looked forward to all year, and different expectations make a ruined holiday for one of you. It works out very well when you know in advance.
parler: What was your best holiday ever, and why?
What if we split it: part of the trip your way, part of it mine?
tps6.eviter: Booking without asking, even as a surprise.

tps7.q: Little gestures (a note, a small gift, a message during the day) are...
tps7.pourquoi: We don't all show love the same way. For some, a message at lunchtime counts more than a big present, and the other has no idea it's missing.
parler: What was the last little gesture that really made you happy?
What could I do more often that wouldn't cost me anything?
tps7.eviter: Waiting for the other to guess: what matters to you isn't obvious to them.

o: They must be celebrated, it's sacred
I don't attach importance to them
tps8.pourquoi: Forgetting a date means nothing to one person and hurts the other. It's not the date that matters, it's what it says: "I thought about us".
parler: Which date matters most to you during the year?
How would you like us to celebrate the next one?
tps8.eviter: Saying "it's just commercial" when it matters to the other: the point is how they feel, not the holiday.

tps9.q: Doing things together you've never done before (a new place, an activity, a different kind of trip), you'd like to do...
tps9.pourquoi: Couples who regularly share new experiences get less bored in their relationship, and boredom wears a couple down long before arguments do. You still need the same appetite for novelty: for one of you it's an adventure, for the other it's one more thing to organise.
parler: What's the last thing we did together for the very first time?
What would you like us to try this year?
tps9.eviter: Planning a "surprise" that the other will experience as yet another chore.

entourage.intro: Your families, the holidays, your friends, nights out without the other. Everything around your relationship.

rapport.fort: You see your families and friends the same way. The holidays should go smoothly!
rapport.moyen: A few differences on the place of family and friends. Nothing unusual, everyone brings their own habits, but it's worth laying them out before the next family gathering.
rapport.faible: Family and friends are a sensitive topic for you. It's almost never about the people themselves, more about their place: who comes first, and when.

ent1.q: Seeing your families (yours and {autre}'s), you'd like to...
ent1.qNeutre: Seeing your families (yours and your partner's), you'd like to...
ent1.pourquoi: Everyone comes with their family, and every family has its habits. The one who sees theirs often finds it normal, the other can feel it takes up all the space.
parler: What do you like about my family, and what's hard for you?
How many weekends a month do you think is reasonable to spend with our families?
ent1.eviter: Criticising the other's family: you're allowed to criticise your own, rarely to hear the other do it.

ent2.q: If your family criticises {autre} in front of you, you...
ent2.qNeutre: If your family criticises your partner in front of you, you...
o: I stand up for {autre} straight away
I talk to my family about it later
I say nothing at the time
oNeutre: I stand up for my partner straight away
I talk to my family about it later
I say nothing at the time
ent2.court: Standing up for each other with family
ent2.pourquoi: It's not what the in-laws say that hurts most, it's your partner's silence. Knowing the other will stand up for you changes everything.
parler: Was there a time you wished I'd said something and I didn't?
How would you like me to react when it happens?
ent2.eviter: Answering "they didn't mean any harm": maybe not, but it still hurt.

ent3.q: The end-of-year holidays, ideally, you spend them...
ent3.pourquoi: Christmas is one of the big moments of tension for couples: two families, one evening, and traditions each person holds on to without always saying so.
parler: What matters most to you at Christmas: the place, the people, or a particular moment?
What if we decided now for the next three years?
ent3.eviter: Waiting until December to talk about it: under pressure, everyone defends their side.

ent4.q: Your friends and {autre}'s friends, you like to see them...
ent4.qNeutre: Your friends and your partner's friends, you like to see them...
ent4.pourquoi: Some people dream of one shared group, others want to keep their friends to themselves. Both are fine, but the one who's never invited to the other's friends can feel left out.
parler: Which of my friends do you feel most comfortable with?
Are there friends you'd rather see without me? That's fine, tell me which ones.
ent4.eviter: Bringing your friends to every outing, or never inviting the other at all.

ent5.q: When {autre} goes out without you (an evening, a weekend with friends), you find it...
ent5.qNeutre: When your partner goes out without you (an evening, a weekend with friends), you find it...
o: Normal, whenever they feel like it
ent5.pourquoi: It's not the evening that's the problem, it's what you imagine during it. Agreeing on what's normal stops every night out from turning into a negotiation.
parler: What would reassure you when I go out without you?
One night out with friends a week, a month: what feels normal to you?
ent5.eviter: Saying "go on" while making it clear you're not OK with it.

ent6.q: Taking in an elderly parent who can no longer live alone, one day:
ent6.pourquoi: It's a question nobody asks at thirty, and it comes up one day without warning. In some families it's obvious, in others it's unthinkable.
parler: How did it go with the grandparents in your family?
If it happened tomorrow with one of our parents, what would we actually do?
ent6.eviter: Promising something to your family before talking to the other.

ent7.q: What happens in your relationship, you tell the people close to you...
ent7.pourquoi: Confiding feels good, but the other can feel very hurt to find out your friends know every detail of your arguments. Everyone has their limit, better to know it.
parler: What wouldn't you want me to tell anyone, even close friends?
Who do you confide in when things aren't going well between us?
ent7.eviter: Telling friends about an argument before you've talked about it together.

travail.intro: The place work has in your life, your plans, and what you're ready to change for the other.

rapport.fort: You give work the same place in your lives. That saves you the feeling of coming second to the other's job.
rapport.moyen: Your ambitions are a little different, which is pretty normal. What matters most is that each of you knows what the other would like to be doing in five years.
rapport.faible: Work doesn't carry the same weight for the two of you. For one it may be a passion, for the other a way to make a living. Both are perfectly respectable, as long as you know it.

tra1.q: In your life, work has a place that's...
o: Central, it's a big part of who I am
Secondary, it's mostly to pay the bills
tra1.pourquoi: When work matters enormously to one of you and little to the other, the first feels misunderstood and the second neglected. There's no right answer, just two ways of living to fit together.
parler: What do you really like about your job?
Are there times when you feel my work comes before you?
tra1.eviter: Saying "it's just a job" to someone for whom it isn't just a job.

tra2.q: Working evenings or weekends, for you, is...
o: Normal if the job requires it
tra2.pourquoi: Evening emails and Sunday files eat into your time together without you noticing. What's normal for one is an absence for the other.
parler: Which moment of the week would you like to keep work-free, whatever happens?
When I work in the evening, how does it feel for you?
tra2.eviter: Promising to "never" work in the evening again: better a rule you'll actually keep.

tra3.q: Changing careers or going back to studying, even if it means earning less for a while:
o: Why not, if the plan is solid
tra3.pourquoi: A career change is rarely done alone: it's the couple that carries the drop in income and the uncertainty. Knowing whether the other would follow saves you from keeping a plan secret for years.
parler: If you could do any job tomorrow, what would it be?
How much could we cut our budget for a year if one of us went for it?
tra3.eviter: Discouraging the other from the first words: you can have worries and still listen to the end.

tra4.q: Earning a lot of money is, for you...
tra4.pourquoi: The money you want to earn often says what you expect from life: security, freedom, success, or none of those. Two very different ambitions end up pulling a couple in two directions.
parler: What would you do with a lot more money?
What would you be willing to give up to earn more?
tra4.eviter: Calling the other's ambition materialistic, or their lack of ambition lazy.

tra5.q: In the evening, talking about your workday, you need it...
tra5.court: Talking about work in the evening
tra5.pourquoi: For one person, telling their day is how they let it go. For the other, it's living it again. Someone who needs to talk and runs into someone who wants to switch off ends up alone with their worries.
parler: When you tell me about your day, do you want my opinion, or for me to just listen?
Shall we give ourselves a moment to talk about it, then switch off?
tra5.eviter: Offering solutions when the other just needs to talk.

tra6.q: If one of you earns a lot more than the other, for you...
o: It might change a few small things
It would bother me a lot
tra6.pourquoi: A pay gap often changes more than people think: who decides, who pays for what, who feels they owe something. Talking about it while things are fine is much easier than when it's already causing friction.
parler: If one of us earned twice as much as the other, what would change for us?
Have you ever felt uncomfortable about money between us?
tra6.eviter: Making the one who earns less feel like they "cost" the couple.

tra7.q: Starting a project together (a business, an activity, a charity):
o: Rather not, I prefer to keep couple and work apart
tra7.pourquoi: Some couples dream of building something together, others want the relationship to stay a refuge. Knowing where the other stands saves you from proposing a project that scares them.
parler: If we had to start a project together, what would it be?
What would scare you about working with me?
tra7.eviter: Dragging the other into your project on the assumption they'll love it.

argent.intro: Joint account or not, splitting costs, saving. Money is one of the topics couples avoid most, so here's your chance.

rapport.fort: You see money the same way. That's a real asset, because it's one of the first things couples argue about.
rapport.moyen: You mostly agree on money, with a few things to settle. Best to talk about it on a day when everything's fine, not the day of a big purchase.
rapport.faible: Money doesn't mean the same thing to the two of you. Behind it there are often two different fears: running short, or not enjoying life. A clear system, decided together, calms a lot of things down.

arg1.q: Your money as a couple, ideally...
o: A joint account for shared costs, the rest our own
Separate money, we split the bills
arg1.pourquoi: There's no right way to organise it, just the one that suits you both. It gets tricky when one of you sees separate accounts as distrust and the other sees a joint account as a loss of freedom.
parler: How did your parents handle money?
What makes you feel safe, with money?
arg1.eviter: Making it about trust ("don't you trust me?"): it's often just a matter of habit.

arg2.q: Shared costs (rent, groceries, going out), for you, are split...
o: The one who earns more pays more, no calculating
arg2.pourquoi: Fifty-fifty seems fair, until the day one earns twice as much as the other and the second has nothing left. Splitting by income seems fair too, but some people feel it turns love into accounting.
parler: At the end of the month, how much is left for you, and for me?
What would feel fairest to you, and why?
arg2.eviter: Keeping accounts to the penny without talking about it: when the other finds out, it feels like distrust.

arg3.q: For a purchase over €300 just for yourself...
o: I make it without mentioning it
oNeutre: I make it without mentioning it
arg3.pourquoi: It's not the amount that upsets people, it's finding out about the purchase afterwards. Setting a threshold together avoids both feeling watched and nasty surprises.
parler: Above what amount would you like us to talk first?
Was there a purchase of mine that made you wince?
arg3.eviter: Hiding a purchase: when it comes out, it becomes a question of trust.

o: Not a priority, you have to enjoy life
arg4.pourquoi: The saver sees the other's spending as carelessness, the spender sees the other's saving as life put off until later. They're often two different fears: running short, or not living.
parler: What would worry you about money in ten years?
How much could we put aside each month without depriving ourselves?
arg4.eviter: Judging the other's spending without knowing what it means to them.

arg5.q: €1,000 out of the blue, what would you do with it?
o: A trip or an outing together
arg5.pourquoi: This low-stakes question says a lot about what money means to each of you: security, memories, comfort or freedom.
parler: What if we really treated ourselves, with part of our savings?
What makes you happier: buying something or doing something?
arg5.eviter: Making fun of the other's choice: there's no wrong answer here.

o: Easy, we talk about it often
arg6.pourquoi: Money is one of the subjects couples avoid most, and a subject you avoid always comes back at the wrong moment. If one of you finds it easy and the other complicated, maybe one talks and the other keeps quiet.
parler: What makes you uncomfortable when we talk about money?
How often shall we do a calm money check-in?
arg6.eviter: Only talking about money when there's a problem.

arg7.q: Who handles most of the couple's money (budget, bills, paperwork, taxes)?
arg7.pourquoi: The one who handles the paperwork carries an invisible load, and the one who handles nothing often doesn't know where the couple stands. It becomes a real problem the day something big and unexpected happens.
parler: Would you know where to find our important papers if I wasn't around?
Would you like us to share the admin differently?
arg7.eviter: Letting the other handle everything, then criticising their choices.

arg7b.q: When you're together (going out, restaurants, weekends), who pays most often?
arg7b.court: Who pays when you go out
arg7b.pourquoi: Without a shared home, the couple's money is mostly the money spent going out. The one who almost always pays ends up noticing; the one who almost never pays often doesn't.
parler: Do you think what each of us puts in when we go out is fair?
What do we do when one of us earns clearly less than the other?
arg7b.eviter: Keeping a tally of every bill in your head without ever talking about it.

arg8.q: Helping a family member financially, even with a large sum:
o: No, not for a large sum
arg8.pourquoi: In some families, helping your own is a given. In others, money isn't lent. When money is shared, it's no longer only the decision of the person whose family it is.
parler: If someone in your family asked you for money tomorrow, what would you do?
Up to what amount would you find it normal to help without talking first?
arg8.eviter: Secretly helping your family with the couple's money.

logement.intro: Moving in, city or countryside, buying, leaving. The decisions you can't split down the middle.

rapport.fort: You see yourselves living in the same place, in the same way. For big decisions, that's a solid base.
rapport.moyen: You broadly agree on where and how to live, with a few nuances. They become real questions the day a decision comes up, so better to talk about them before.
rapport.faible: You don't necessarily see yourselves in the same place, or living the same way. These are decisions you can't split down the middle, so better to talk about them long before you have to choose.

log1.pourquoi: One has been waiting for the question for months, the other has never really thought about it: it's a very common gap, and better discovered before the waiting turns into resentment.
parler: What makes you want to live together, and what scares you?
What would need to be sorted before we move in?
log1.eviter: Hearing "not right now" as "not with you".

log2.q: In ten years, you see yourself living...
o: In a mid-sized town or the suburbs
log2.court: Where to live in ten years
log2.pourquoi: City or countryside isn't just about scenery: it's a job, a school, friends, a pace of life. It can't be split down the middle, hence the point of talking about it well before you start looking.
parler: If we could live anywhere with no work constraints, where would it be?
What would you miss most if we left here?
log2.eviter: Putting the question off with "we'll see": the day it comes up, you often have to decide fast.

log3.pourquoi: For one, buying means building something and feeling secure. For the other, it means twenty-five years of debt and lost freedom. Both views make sense, but they don't lead to the same life.
parler: What does buying mean to you: security, success, something else?
How many more years do you see us renting?
log3.eviter: Starting viewings to convince the other.

log3b.q: Your current home, for the years ahead...
o: It still suits us for a while
I'd like to leave as soon as possible
log3b.pourquoi: A home you bought together is somewhere you either get attached to or feel stuck in. If one dreams of leaving and the other sees it as the home of a lifetime, better to know.
parler: What's missing in our home for you?
Where do you see us living in five years?
log3b.eviter: Waiting for the next big decision (a baby, a new job) to talk about it.

log4.q: Living close to your families is...
log4.pourquoi: Near family, you have help, Sunday lunches and grandparents round the corner. Far away, you have more freedom. And when the two families live hundreds of miles apart, the question quickly becomes: near which one?
parler: How far from your parents would you like us to live?
What do you like about being far from, or close to, your family?
log4.eviter: Settling near your family on the assumption the other will follow.

log5.qNeutre: Moving far away for your partner's job:
o: Yes, if it's a great opportunity
log5.pourquoi: A great job offer in another city often comes out of nowhere. If one assumes the other will follow and the other has never considered leaving, the offer becomes a choice between the relationship and a career.
parler: For what kind of opportunity would you leave here?
What would you ask in return if you followed me?
log5.eviter: Applying far away without talking first, "just to see".

log6.pourquoi: Living somewhere else is a dream for some and an uprooting for others. It's the kind of plan people keep to themselves until the right moment, and that surprises the other the day it's said out loud.
parler: Is there a country where you could see yourself living?
What keeps you here?
log6.eviter: Brushing off the other's dream in one sentence: you can say no to a plan and still respect the wish.

log7.q: At home, who decides most about decor and layout?
log7.pourquoi: The one who never chooses anything can end up not feeling at home. The one who chooses everything sometimes feels the other doesn't care.
parler: Is there a corner of the home you'd like to set up your way?
What would you change first in our place?
log7.eviter: Changing the decor without asking, even as a surprise.

enfants.intro: Wanting them or not, when, how many, how to raise them. Or, if you already have them, how you organise things.

rapport.fort: On children, you're on the same wavelength. It's probably the topic where that matters most.
rapport.moyen: You're close on children, with differences in timing or approach. They're easy to work out when you talk about them early.
rapport.faible: You don't have the same wishes or ideas about children. It's the topic where compromise is hardest, so you need to talk about it openly, without counting on time to change the other's mind.

enf1.pourquoi: It's the question that can't be negotiated: you can't have half a child. Many couples have never asked it openly, each thinking the other will eventually want them... or give up.
parler: What makes you want children, or what pulls you away from the idea?
If one of us really didn't want them, what would we do?
enf1.eviter: Counting on time to change the other's mind.

enf2.q: A first child, ideally, would be...
enf2.pourquoi: Wanting a child isn't enough to agree: one thinks "next year", the other "in five years", and the years go by. Age sometimes puts a deadline on this question.
parler: What would need to be in place before having a child, for you?
Do you have an age limit in mind?
enf2.eviter: Putting it off without giving a date: for the one who's waiting, "later" means nothing.

enf3.pourquoi: An only child or a big family isn't the same house, the same budget or the same life. The idea often comes from your own childhood, to repeat it or to do the opposite.
parler: Did you like being an only child, or having brothers and sisters?
Where does that number come from, for you?
enf3.eviter: Setting a number like a promise: life decides too.

enf1b.pourquoi: After a child, wishes often change, and not always in the same direction for both. One has found a balance, the other is already thinking about the next.
parler: What makes you want, or fear, the idea of another child?
What would change for you day to day?
enf1b.eviter: Talking about it exhausted after a bad night, or charmed by a friend's baby.

enf2b.q: Since you've had children, time just for the two of you...
enf2b.pourquoi: It's what research shows most clearly after a birth: the couple moves to the back, and years later struggles to get to the front again. The couples that last are the ones who keep moments for two, even short ones.
parler: What counts as real time for the two of us right now, for you?
What could we set aside every week, just us?
enf2b.eviter: Waiting for the children to grow up before looking after the couple.

enf3b.q: With the children, you are two parents who...
o: Complement each other: one firmer, the other softer
Each do things their own way
One of whom makes most of the decisions
enf3b.pourquoi: Researchers call it co-parenting: not necessarily the same parenting style, but the feeling of being a team. It's what weighs most on the couple once the children are there, far more than the number of nappies changed.
parler: Do you feel backed up by me in front of the children?
What do we contradict each other about most often in front of them?
enf3b.eviter: Settling a parenting disagreement in front of the children, with one of them as a witness.

enf4.q: When it comes to raising a child, you're more...
enf4.pourquoi: Two parents with different ideas about authority often end up playing good cop and bad cop, and the child quickly learns who to ask. You don't need the same upbringing, but you do need to agree on a few rules.
parler: What would you keep from how your parents raised you, and what wouldn't you do again?
Which rule would you never give in on?
enf4.eviter: Contradicting the other in front of the child.

enf5.q: With the children (daily life, homework, doctor, nights), who does, or would do, the most?
enf5.pourquoi: Even in couples who want to share equally, a baby often tips the load onto one side, within a few months and without anyone deciding it.
parler: Concretely, in a typical week with a child, who would do what?
What would you absolutely want to do yourself with our children?
enf5.eviter: Saying you "help" the other with the kids: a parent doesn't help, they do their share.

enf6.q: Cutting down your working hours (part-time, a break) to look after the children:
enf6.court: Cutting back work for the kids
enf6.pourquoi: When one person cuts back, it's often their career and pension that pay the price for years. Better that it's a choice you both know about, rather than something that just slides.
parler: If one of us had to slow down, who would it be, and why?
How would we make up for it for the one earning less?
enf6.eviter: Assuming it's automatically the lower earner who stops.

enf7.q: Grandparents in the children's lives, you want them...
o: Very present, every day if possible
enf7.pourquoi: Grandparents are a precious help, and sometimes a source of tension: unrequested advice, different rules, unannounced visits. People often accept from their own parents what they wouldn't stand from their in-laws.
parler: What would you accept from my parents with our children, and what wouldn't you?
And from yours?
enf7.eviter: Letting your own parents ignore the rules you set together.

enf8.q: In a blended family, raising the other's children is...
o: Both our business, but the parent has the last word
enf8.pourquoi: The step-parent never quite knows how far they're allowed to step in, and the parent hesitates between asking for help and protecting their children. Clarifying roles is a relief for everyone, starting with the children.
parler: What do you expect from me with your children, concretely?
Are there things you'd rather I didn't do?
enf8.eviter: Turning the children's upbringing into a competition with the ex.

enf9.q: If your partner started wanting a child, you would...
o: See it as a real problem between us
Talk about it, but I don't think I'd change my mind
enf9.court: If the other changes their mind
enf9.pourquoi: Not wanting children is a decision most people make early and that changes little with age. But in a couple, it only takes one of the two to change for everything to be back on the table.
parler: What could make you change your mind, if anything?
If one of us changed their mind, what would we do?
enf9.eviter: Assuming the other will end up wanting the same thing as you.

enf10.q: When family or friends ask "so, when are the kids coming?", you...
o: Say clearly that it isn't planned
Dodge it, with humour or otherwise
enf10.pourquoi: Couples who are childfree by choice hear the question for years, from family, colleagues and friends. How each of you feels under that pressure, and how you answer it, says a lot about how solid the choice is as a couple.
parler: Who asks you most often, and what do you answer?
Would you like us to give the same answer, both of us?
enf10.eviter: Letting one of you take the remarks alone.

enf11.q: Without children, the project that matters most to the two of you is...
o: A house, a place of our own
Free time, with no big project
enf11.pourquoi: A childfree couple builds itself around something else: travel, a career, a place, or simply time. When the two don't share the same "something else", one soon feels like they're living the other's project.
parler: In ten years, where do you see us, and doing what?
What do we do with the freedom it leaves us?
enf11.eviter: Filling the time without ever deciding together what to do with it.

enf12.q: Other people's children (nephews, nieces, friends' kids): who most wants to spend time with them?
enf12.pourquoi: Not wanting children says nothing about how you feel around other people's. When one loves being the uncle or the godmother and the other avoids them, family weekends aren't lived the same way.
parler: What do you like, or not, about time spent with our relatives' children?
Being a godparent, would that appeal to you?
enf12.eviter: Imposing on the other a role with relatives' children that they didn't choose.

enf13.q: Growing old without children (who will be there, loneliness, dependence): you think about it...
o: Never, we'll sort it out when the time comes
enf13.pourquoi: It's the argument most often thrown at childfree couples, and research doesn't back it up: older people without children aren't more isolated, provided they've built a circle around them. The two of you still need to think about it the same way.
parler: What would reassure you about later on?
Who will we be able to count on, and who will be able to count on us?
enf13.eviter: Brushing off the other's worry with a "we'll see".

enf14.q: Having someone or something to take care of together (a pet, godchildren, a commitment):
enf14.pourquoi: Many childfree couples put that urge elsewhere: a dog, a garden, godchildren, a charity. When one needs it and the other doesn't, it's a small frustration that lasts.
parler: Do you feel like looking after someone or something at the moment?
What could we have or do together along those lines?
enf14.eviter: Getting a pet for only one of you.

valeurs.intro: Religion, commitment, what matters most to you, and what you want to pass on.

rapport.fort: You share the same values. It's what helps most when you have to make hard decisions.
rapport.moyen: Your values are close, with a few different priorities. They often enrich a couple, as long as each respects the other's.
rapport.faible: You don't put the same things first. You can love each other very well with different values, but you need to know which ones matter most to the other, and what they'll mean in practice.

val1.q: Religion or spirituality, in your life, is...
val1.pourquoi: Two different beliefs can live together very well. The problem is not knowing what the other's faith really means to them, and what it will mean on the day of a wedding, a birth or a funeral.
parler: What does your faith, or lack of faith, bring you day to day?
Are there holidays or rituals you care about?
val1.eviter: Making fun of the other's beliefs, even as a joke.

val2.q: Passing a religion on to your children (baptism, religious education...):
val2.pourquoi: Baptism, circumcision, Sunday school or a religious school come up very quickly after a birth, and that's often when couples find out they didn't think the same at all.
parler: What would you like to pass on to our children, religion or not?
If our families put pressure on us, what would we say?
val2.eviter: Letting the grandparents decide for you.

val2b.q: What you'll leave behind you (a body of work, a business, something passed on to loved ones) matters to you...
val2b.pourquoi: Without children, the question of what you pass on comes up differently: a body of work, knowledge, a place, a commitment, or nothing in particular. Two people who don't give it the same importance won't make the same life choices.
parler: What would you like to leave, or pass on, and to whom?
Does it matter to you that we build something bigger than us?
val2b.eviter: Reducing everything you pass on to children: there are other ways.

val3.q: Marriage or a civil partnership, for you...
val3.pourquoi: For one person, getting married is obvious or a dream. For the other, it's a piece of paper that changes nothing, or an institution they don't believe in. The misunderstanding often lasts for years, with expectation on one side and no idea of it on the other.
parler: What would marriage mean to you?
If there were a wedding, what would it look like?
val3.eviter: Joking about a proposal when the other is really waiting for one.

val3b.q: The commitment you made (marriage or civil partnership), for you, is...
o: As long as we're happy together
A piece of paper that doesn't change much
val3b.pourquoi: The same "yes" doesn't mean the same thing to everyone. Knowing what commitment means to the other helps you understand how they live through the hard times.
parler: What did that "yes" mean to you, the day we said it?
What has changed for you since?
val3b.eviter: Using the commitment as an argument in a fight.

val4.q: Ecology in your daily life (shopping, food, transport):
o: A priority, I make a lot of effort
Important, I do what I can
I think about it, nothing more
val4.pourquoi: Ecology has become a real couple topic: flying on holiday, meat, the car, what you buy. It's not just an opinion, it's choices made every day, together.
parler: Is there an effort you'd like us to make together?
What wouldn't you want to be forced to change?
val4.eviter: Lecturing at every meal or every purchase.

val5.q: What matters most in your life:
val5.pourquoi: You can love each other and not put the same thing first. What matters most to each person decides the hard choices: a job far away, an overbearing family, a risky project.
parler: Why did you pick that first?
What would you put second?
val5.eviter: Taking the other's answer as a ranking of your relationship.

val6.q: A small lie to avoid an argument or not to hurt the other is...
val6.pourquoi: Some people see the slightest bending of the truth as a betrayal, others as a kindness. The day a little lie comes out, that difference decides how big the argument gets.
parler: Are there things you'd rather not know?
Would you rather have a truth that hurts or a lie that protects?
val6.eviter: Snooping to check: it settles the question of one lie and opens another, about trust.

o: I care about them a lot
I go along without caring much
val7.pourquoi: Traditions are often what's most tied to childhood. Someone who happily does without them can unknowingly hurt someone for whom a ritual means a lot.
parler: Which tradition from your family would you like us to keep?
What if we invented our own?

val8.q: Having the same political views as {autre} is...
val8.qNeutre: Having the same political views as your partner is...
val8.pourquoi: Some couples never talk politics, others debate every night. It gets tricky when one sees it as a matter of values and the other as just an opinion.
parler: Is there a social issue we could never agree on?
What hurts you when we debate?
val8.eviter: Debating to win: in a couple, whoever wins the debate often loses the evening.

disputes.intro: How you say what's wrong, how you argue, and how you make up.

rapport.fort: You handle tension the same way. You argue like everyone does, but you understand each other when it happens.
rapport.moyen: You don't handle arguments quite the same way. Knowing what the other needs when things heat up already changes a lot.
rapport.faible: You have two very different ways of living through a disagreement. Often one wants to sort it out right away and the other needs to step back, and each makes the other's fear worse without meaning to. It's the area where a bit of method helps most.

dis1.q: When something about {autre} bothers you, you say so...
dis1.qNeutre: When something about your partner bothers you, you say so...
o: Fairly soon, at the right moment
Rarely, I keep it to myself
dis1.pourquoi: Someone who says things straight away and someone who bottles them up don't understand each other: the first thinks everything's fine since the other says nothing, the second ends up exploding over a detail.
parler: Is there something you've been keeping to yourself for a while?
How can I make it easier for you to tell me?
dis1.eviter: Answering a criticism with another one ("what about you?").

dis2.q: During an argument, what you need is...
o: To sort it out right away
A break to calm down before talking
To let it pass, it'll sort itself out
dis2.pourquoi: One needs to settle the argument straight away to feel better, the other needs to step away so as not to say something stupid. The first pushes, the second leaves, and each makes the other's fear grow.
parler: When I leave the room during an argument, how does that feel for you?
Shall we agree on a signal to say "pause, let's talk again in an hour"?
dis2.eviter: Following the other from room to room, or leaving without saying when you'll be back.

o: Never, we sort it out first
dis3.pourquoi: For some people, going to bed angry is unthinkable. Others sort things out better after a night's sleep. Both make sense, but the other needs to know.
parler: What helps you sleep after an argument?
Can we say goodnight, even when we're angry?
dis3.eviter: Forcing a discussion at two in the morning, when nobody can listen anymore.

dis4.q: After an argument, who usually makes the first move?
dis4.court: The first move after an argument
dis4.pourquoi: The one who always makes the first move ends up feeling they always give in, even when they were right. Making the first move isn't admitting you're wrong, it's saying you care about the other.
parler: How do you know when I want to make peace?
What helps you come back to me?
dis4.eviter: Waiting for the other to come to you to prove you were right.

dis5.q: Raising your voice during an argument, for you, is...
o: Just another way of expressing yourself
dis5.pourquoi: In some families, people shout and forget. In others, a raised voice is already frightening. The same rising tone doesn't carry the same weight for both of you.
parler: How did people argue at your parents' place?
At what point does an argument become too much for you?
dis5.eviter: Saying "I'm not shouting, I'm just talking loudly": it's the person in front of you who knows how it lands.

dis6.q: When things aren't going well, what helps you most is...
o: Being left alone for a while
dis6.court: What helps when things are hard
dis6.pourquoi: We often comfort the other the way we'd like to be comforted ourselves: by talking, offering solutions, giving a hug. It misses the mark when the other needs something else.
parler: The last time things weren't going well for you, what would have helped?
How can I tell what you need in the moment?
dis6.eviter: Offering solutions to someone who just needs to be listened to.

dis7.q: Saying "I love you", "thank you" or "sorry", for you, is...
dis7.pourquoi: Some people show love with words, others with actions, often without realising it. Someone who needs to hear it can have doubts, even with a thousand proofs.
parler: Which word would you like to hear more often from me?
How do you tell me you love me, without saying it?
dis7.eviter: Assuming the other already knows: knowing and hearing aren't the same.

dis8.q: During your arguments, criticism sometimes targets the person rather than the problem ("you always...", "you never..."):
dis8.pourquoi: Saying "you forgot the shopping" is about a fact. Saying "you never think of anything" is about the person, and the other has only one option left: to defend themselves. Researchers who have watched couples for decades see this shift as one of the first signs an argument is going to go badly.
parler: When I criticise something, how could I say it so it doesn't feel like an attack?
Is there something I say that always makes you tense up?

dis9.q: During an argument, one of you sometimes mocks the other, is sarcastic or rolls their eyes:
dis9.pourquoi: Contempt (sarcasm, mockery, eye-rolling) is, in studies that follow couples over many years, the most worrying signal for a relationship's future. It tells the other "I'm better than you", which no disagreement ever says.
parler: Do I sometimes use a tone that hurts you, even as a joke?
What do you admire about me, even when you're angry?

dis10.q: When {autre} criticises you, your first reflex is to justify yourself or hit back with another criticism:
dis10.pourquoi: Justifying yourself is a very human reflex. The problem is that the other hears "it's not my fault" and repeats the complaint louder. Acknowledging even a small part ("you're right, I forgot") is often enough to bring the tension down.
parler: When I justify myself, what would you need to hear instead?
On what topic do you feel I never admit anything?

dis11.q: During an argument, one of you sometimes shuts down completely: stops answering, leaves the room without a word, or acts as if the other wasn't there:
dis11.pourquoi: Shutting down is almost never indifference: it's often the body overloading, the heart beating too fast to think. But for the person left facing it, that silence feels like a wall. A real break of about twenty minutes, announced with a time to come back, makes a big difference.
parler: When I shut down, how does it feel for you?
Shall we agree on a word for "break, I need twenty minutes"?

dis12.q: After an argument, you manage to make up (a gesture, a joke, a "sorry", a hug):
dis12.pourquoi: Every couple argues. According to research, couples who last have as many arguments as others; the difference is that they find it easier to come back to each other afterwards, with a gesture, a word or a joke.
parler: What works best for you when we make up?
Is there an argument we've never really got over?

confiance.intro: Phones, exes, jealousy, and what each of you calls cheating.

rapport.fort: You have the same idea of trust and fidelity. Many couples have never said it out loud. Now you know.
rapport.moyen: You agree on the essentials, with a few lines drawn in different places. Better to know them before a situation reveals them.
rapport.faible: You don't draw the lines in the same place. It doesn't mean there's a problem today, but the same gesture could be harmless to one of you and a betrayal to the other.

con1.q: Looking at {autre}'s phone, for you, is...
con1.qNeutre: Looking at your partner's phone, for you, is...
o: No, each to their own phone
con1.pourquoi: For one person, an open phone is proof of trust. For the other, it's a phone you don't look at that proves it. So the same gesture can reassure one and hurt the other.
parler: Is there something on my phone that worries you?
What would reassure you more than looking?
con1.eviter: Looking in secret: what you find matters less than the fact you looked.

con2.q: For you, cheating starts when you...
con2.pourquoi: Two people can be completely faithful by their own definition and cheat by the other's. It's often only afterwards that you discover you didn't have the same line.
parler: Are there things that aren't cheating for you, but would still hurt?
If an ex messaged me, would you want me to tell you?
con2.eviter: Mocking the other's line because you find it too strict.

con3.q: Staying in touch with an ex:
con3.pourquoi: Some people stay friends with their exes, others cut all ties. The one who keeps in touch doesn't see the problem, the one who never would sees a door left open.
parler: What would reassure you if I stayed in touch with an ex?
Is there one ex in particular who makes you uneasy?
con3.eviter: Hiding a conversation with an ex, even a harmless one.

con4.q: {autre} having a very close friend, the kind they could be attracted to:
con4.qNeutre: Your partner having a very close friend, the kind they could be attracted to:
con4.pourquoi: Friendship between two people who could be attracted to each other is obvious to some and dangerous to others. The unease rarely comes from the friendship itself, more from what you don't know about it.
parler: Is there a friendship on my side that makes you uncomfortable?
What would help you feel at ease with that person?
con4.eviter: Brushing off the other's unease with "that's ridiculous".

con5.q: Jealousy in a couple, for you, is...
o: A sign you care about each other
Something to keep an eye on
con5.pourquoi: For some, a bit of jealousy proves you care. For others, it's a lack of trust. Someone who finds it flattering can, without meaning to, provoke someone who experiences it as a prison.
parler: What makes you jealous, even a little?
How can I reassure you without it turning into surveillance?
con5.eviter: Making the other jealous on purpose, "just to see".

con6.qNeutre: Knowing your partner's codes and passwords:
o: Goes without saying, we share everything
con6.pourquoi: Sharing your codes can be proof of trust or just a precaution in an emergency. Not sharing them can be modesty or a wish for some space of your own. What matters is knowing what it means to the other.
parler: Are there codes we should both know, in case something happens?
What would you like to keep just for yourself?
con6.eviter: Demanding a code as proof of love.

con7.q: An open relationship (seeing other people, with the other's agreement):
con7.pourquoi: It's rarely said out loud, yet some people do want it. Knowing, even to say no, stops it turning into infidelity or a fantasy kept to yourself for years.
parler: What attracts you, or scares you, about the idea?
Is it a real wish, or more of a curiosity?
con7.eviter: Judging the other for answering honestly: that's exactly what will stop the next honest answer.

o: It would depend on what happened
con8.pourquoi: Nobody really knows what they'd do. But knowing what the other thinks today says a lot about what matters to them, and how serious a slip would be.
parler: What would be hardest to forgive for you: the act, or the lie?
Is there something you'd never forgive me?
con8.eviter: Taking the other's answer as permission.

intimite.intro: Desire, tenderness, and how you talk about them. Only {autre} will see these answers.

rapport.fort: You have the same desires and the same way of living them. That's precious, and it needs looking after.
rapport.moyen: Your desires are close, with a few differences. Talking about it calmly, on a quiet day, often helps more than anything else.
rapport.faible: Your desires don't always meet. It's one of the most common and least discussed topics in couples: what matters is that neither of you lives with it alone.

int1.pourquoi: Different levels of desire are one of the first reasons couples give for breaking up. It's not a problem in itself, it's the silence around it that makes it one: the one who wants more feels rejected, the one who wants less feels pressured.
parler: What puts you in the mood, outside the bedroom?
What puts you off at the moment?
int1.eviter: Keeping count, or comparing yourselves to other couples.

int2.q: Everyday tenderness (cuddles, gestures, kisses with no ulterior motive), you'd like...
int2.pourquoi: When every tender gesture is taken as an invitation, the one who isn't in the mood ends up avoiding tenderness too. Separating the two often brings both back.
parler: Which tender gesture do you like most?
Are there times you'd just like a cuddle, with nothing after?
int2.eviter: Turning every cuddle into an invitation.

int3.q: Talking about your sex life together is...
o: Easy, we talk about it often
int3.pourquoi: Many couples make love for years without ever telling each other what they like. Couples who talk about it aren't more liberated, they've just got used to it.
parler: What would make this conversation easier for you?
Is there something you've never dared to tell me?
int3.eviter: Talking about it right after a moment that didn't go well: it's gentler when things are calm.

int4.q: Who most often makes the first move?
int4.pourquoi: The one who always makes the first move ends up wondering if they're desired, and the one who never does sometimes simply never gets the chance.
parler: How would you feel if I made the first move more often?
How do you let me know you're in the mood, without saying it?
int4.eviter: Taking a "not tonight" as a rejection of you as a person.

int5.pourquoi: One person's wish for something new can feel like a reproach to the other ("are you bored with me?"). It almost never is.
parler: Is there something you've never dared suggest?
What would make you feel comfortable trying?
int5.eviter: Insisting after a no: a wish is something you suggest, not something you negotiate.

int6.pourquoi: Feeling desired is a need, not a whim. You can love each other a lot and stop showing it, and the other ends up thinking they're no longer attractive.
parler: What makes you feel that I desire you?
What could I do more often?

int7.q: Your intimate life at the moment, you find it...
int7.pourquoi: It's not frequency that makes a fulfilling intimate life, it's both people finding what they need in it. When one is satisfied and the other isn't, the first often doesn't know.
parler: What do you miss most?
What do you like, and want us to keep?

int8.q: When your desires don't match, you take it...
int8.pourquoi: Not being in the mood at the same time is the most ordinary thing in the world. What does the damage is how the no is said and received.
parler: How would you like me to say "not tonight"?
What helps you not take it personally?

meteo.intro: To finish, eight questions about how you feel in your relationship right now. There's no agreement to find here, just say how it's going.

met1.q: Right now, in your relationship, you're...
met1.pourquoi: Every couple goes through happier and harder periods. What matters is that both of you know where the other stands, especially when it's not in the same place.
parler: What would do you good right now, in our relationship?
When was our best period, for you?

met2.pourquoi: Feeling listened to is one of the needs couples mention most, and lack of communication is the first reason they give for breaking up.
parler: Is there a topic where you feel I don't listen to you?
What do I do when you feel I'm not listening?

met3.q: When you're going through a hard time, you feel supported by {autre}:
met3.pourquoi: It's in hard times that you see what a couple is made of. Feeling alone when things are bad leaves marks long after.
parler: The last time things weren't going well for you, did I manage to help the way you needed?
How can I support you when you don't ask for anything?

met4.pourquoi: Admiration is one of the most reliable signs of a couple that lasts. When it fades, it's not necessarily love leaving, but it's worth noticing.
parler: What do you admire about me?
Is there something I do that you've never thought to tell me you love?

met5.q: Your arguments, at the moment, are...
met5.pourquoi: Arguing isn't a bad sign in itself. But when arguments become the background noise of the relationship, it's time to look at what's behind them.
parler: Which topic comes up most in our arguments?
What would help us argue less about that one?

met6.q: With {autre}, you feel free to be yourself:
met6.pourquoi: A relationship where you have to watch everything you say is tiring, even without arguments. Feeling free to be yourself is one of the foundations of trust.
parler: Are there times when you feel you have to be careful with me?
What don't you dare do or say in front of me?

met7.q: In ten years, you see yourself with {autre}:
met7.court: Seeing yourselves together in ten years
met7.pourquoi: Picturing yourselves together is one of the most reliable signs that a couple is doing well. A doubt doesn't mean it's over, it means it needs talking about.
parler: How do you picture us in ten years?
What makes you doubt, at the moment?

met8.q: If you had to do it all again, you'd choose {autre} again:
met8.court: If you had to do it again
met8.pourquoi: It's the most direct question in the check-up. An answer that hurts to read is often an answer that was hard to say, and saying it is already a first step.
parler: What would make you answer "yes, without hesitating"?
What has changed since the beginning, for you?

met9.q: When you share good news with {autre}, their reaction is usually...
o: Enthusiastic: we talk about it, they're happy for me
met9.pourquoi: People talk a lot about support in hard times. Research shows that how you react to good news matters at least as much: a "that's great, tell me everything!" brings you closer, a distracted "oh, nice" pushes you apart without you noticing.
parler: What's the last good news you told me, and how did I react?
What shows you that I'm really happy for you?

met10.q: You feel appreciated by {autre}, for what you do and for who you are:
met10.pourquoi: Feeling appreciated by your partner is among the best predictors of relationship quality, according to a large analysis that brought together dozens of couple studies. And appreciation spreads: the person who feels appreciated tends to appreciate the other in return.
parler: What do I do for you that you'd like me to notice more often?
When did you last feel I really saw what you do?

met11.q: You're sure {autre} cares about your relationship as much as you do:
met11.pourquoi: Feeling that the other is truly committed is, in large analyses of couple data, one of the best indicators of relationship quality. A doubt about it often weighs silently, without ever being said.
parler: What shows you that I care about us?
Have there been times when you doubted my commitment?

met12.q: You feel {autre} knows what's going on in your life right now (your worries, your plans, what's on your mind):
met12.pourquoi: Knowing what's on the other's mind right now (a difficult colleague, a project, a worry) is one of the foundations of a solid couple. When that knowledge fades, you end up living side by side rather than together, often without a single argument to flag it.
parler: What's taking up most of your head at the moment?
What don't I know about your week?
